Bohemia
bo-HEE-mee-a
n. (the kingdom of the Czechs, the first land in Europe to carry through a reformation, and the first to have one taken away by force)
Latin Boiohaemum, the home of the Boii, a Celtic people; Czech Čechy; German Böhmen.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Bohemia is the kingdom in which a national reformation was carried, held for two hundred years, and then undone. The burning of Hus in 1415 turned a preaching movement into a nation's cause; the Hussite wars that followed broke five crusades, and the Compacts agreed at Basel and proclaimed in 1436 conceded communion in both kinds to the kingdom, the one formal concession Rome ever made to a reforming body before Trent. Out of the wars came two bodies: the Utraquists, who kept the cup and little else, and the Unity of Brethren, gathered from 1457, who kept a disciplined church with its own ministry, its own hymnody and its own press, and who gave the land the Kralice Bible. The Bohemian Confession of 1575 and the Letter of Majesty of 1609 brought the Lutheran, Utraquist and Brethren parties into one legal settlement. It ended in a single afternoon at White Mountain in November 1620. Thirty thousand families went into exile, the Brethren's press and schools were destroyed, and the land was recatholicised so thoroughly that the Czechs call the age that followed the darkness. The dictionary enters Bohemia because it is the proof that a reformation can be genuinely national, genuinely confessed, and still fail to be rooted, and because the Brethren who survived it became the seed of the modern missionary movement.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a kingdom as the territory subject to a king; a compact as an agreement or contract between parties; a remnant as that which is left after a part is taken away; and exile as banishment from one's country.

expand to see more

KINGDOM, n. The territory or country subject to a king; an undivided territory under the dominion of a monarch.

COMPACT, n. An agreement; a contract between parties; a word that signifies an agreement for the performance of some act.

REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.

EXILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country by authority.

UTRAQUIST, n. One who holds that the laity ought to receive the sacrament in both kinds, in bread and in wine.

Key Scripture

Rom 11:5 — "Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace."

Heb 11:37 — "They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;"

2Ti 3:12 — "Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution."

Psa 22:28 — "For the kingdom is the LORD'S: and he is the governor among the nations."

Modern Corruption

The Czech kingdom, reformed from 1415, settled by the Compacts of 1436 and the Letter of Majesty of 1609, and broken at White Mountain in 1620.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the mistaking of a political victory for a reformation. Bohemia won its wars and got its Compacts, and the Compacts gave the kingdom the cup while leaving the mass, the priesthood, the invocation of saints and purgatory untouched. The Utraquist church that resulted was a church defined by one ceremony and emptied of doctrine, and when the Habsburg pressure came it had almost nothing to resist with. The Unity of Brethren, which had no political settlement at all and was persecuted by Utraquist and Catholic alike, is the body that survived; “there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5) is the right description of it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the measure of a reformation is doctrine taught and discipline kept, not concessions won. Bohemia's exiles are among those of whom it is written that “they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins” (Heb 11:37), and their land's history is the plainest commentary on the warning that “all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12). The kingdom was lost and the church was not, because the church was in the taught people and not in the charter.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek leimma (G3005), a remnant; Greek dioko (G1377), to pursue, to persecute; Hebrew mamlakah (H4467), a kingdom.

expand to see more

Greek leimma (G3005) — a remnant, that which is left; “there is a remnant according to the election of grace”, Romans 11:5.

Greek ekloge (G1589) — a choosing out, election; “the election of grace”, Romans 11:5.

Greek thlibo (G2346) — to press, to afflict; “being destitute, afflicted, tormented”, Hebrews 11:37.

Greek diogmos (G1375) — a persecution, a chasing down; “shall suffer persecution”, 2 Timothy 3:12.

Hebrew mamlakah (H4467) — a kingdom, a realm; “For the kingdom is the LORD'S”, Psalm 22:28.

Usage

"“there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5) — the Unity of Brethren gathered from 1457."

"“they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins” (Heb 11:37) — the thirty thousand families exiled after 1620."

"“For the kingdom is the LORD'S” (Psa 22:28) — a crown lost in an afternoon at White Mountain."
